newsitem.title: FRANCE: France seeks to bury protectionist imaage.
newsitem.headline: France seeks to bury protectionist imaage.

text.p: The French government sought on Tuesday to bury the country's protectionist image, saying it welcomed foreign investment with open arms.

"France was reputed to be a country that was relatively closed and protective," government spokesman Alain Lamassoure told several dozen foreign company executives at an international investors' conference. "That's the past. France has become resolutely open to the world," he said.

France's credentials as a country open to investment were shaken late last year by a government's decision to halt sale of state-owned Thomson Multimedia (TMM) to South Korean conglomerate Daewoo after widespread opposition.
He acknowledged the controversy the Thomson flip-flop had caused but said in an interview that "for every affair that gets into difficulty, there are dozens that succeed."
"Both now and in the future, firms from all over the world wishing to invest in France will be favourably considered by government authorities," he said.
Daewoo Electronics chairman Soon-Hoon Bae, listed among participants at the conference, was not in the audience to hear Lamassoure's comments.
Earlier on Tuesday, Bae renewed criticism of the French decision in an interview in the International Herald Tribune, but said Daewoo was still ready to consider acquiring TMM.

Lamassoure noted France now ranked third among the 27-member OECD for receipt of foreign investment, adding that since the early 1990s, flows of foreign direct investment had exceeded 60 billion francs ($10.5 billion) a year.

He said France's plans to be part of the first wave of a single European currency in 1999 made it a convenient launch pad for penetrating the European market. "Firms which decide to set up in our country will enjoy monetary stability and direct access to a market of 350 million inhabitants," he said.
He added France had cut taxes and social insurance contributions to lure investors. But not all businessmen at the session were sure France was the place to invest.

"The difficulty in France, indeed in all of Europe are the social costs, the lack of flexibility in the workforce. It is a big problem," said Ismail Elmiligy, president of Buckman Laboratories Europe whose European headquarters are in Belgium.
Britain, he said, was a far cheaper place to invest.

But another business executive said France had become a more open environment. "It is an attitudinal change. There's a view they want foreign investment, they want to work with you as a partner. You would not have found this attitude 15 years ago," said Steven Mendell, president and chief executive officer of California-based Prizm pharmaceuticals.
